verses.text: “Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold which they refine.
Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted out of the ore.
Man sets an end to darkness, and searches out, to the furthest bound, the stones of obscurity and of thick darkness.
He breaks open a shaft away from where people live. They are forgotten by the foot. They hang far from men, they swing back and forth.
As for the earth, out of it comes bread; Underneath it is turned up as it were by fire.
Sapphires come from its rocks. It has dust of gold.
That path no bird of prey knows, neither has the falcon’s eye seen it.
The proud animals have not trodden it, nor has the fierce lion passed by there.
He puts his hand on the flinty rock, and he overturns the mountains by the roots.
He cuts out channels among the rocks. His eye sees every precious thing.
He binds the streams that they don’t trickle. The thing that is hidden he brings out to light.
“But where shall wisdom be found? Where is the place of understanding?
Man doesn’t know its price; Neither is it found in the land of the living.
The deep says, ‘It isn’t in me.’ The sea says, ‘It isn’t with me.’
It can’t be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for its price.
It can’t be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire.
Gold and glass can’t equal it, neither shall it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold.
No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal. Yes, the price of wisdom is above rubies.
The topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it, Neither shall it be valued with pure gold.
Where then does wisdom come from? Where is the place of understanding?
Seeing it is hidden from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the birds of the sky.
Destruction and Death say, ‘We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.’
“God understands its way, and he knows its place.
For he looks to the ends of the earth, and sees under the whole sky.
He establishes the force of the wind. Yes, he measures out the waters by measure.
When he made a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunder;
then he saw it, and declared it. He established it, yes, and searched it out.
To man he said, ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord,  that is wisdom. To depart from evil is understanding.’”

footnotes.content: Silver and gold—we dig for them, refine them, spend our lives hunting them. Job opens here with a real place, the mine itself, the crucible where human appetite meets the earth's wealth. How strange that he'll spend the rest of this chapter saying they're worth nothing next to wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Iron, copper—the bones of industry, melted from ore. We shape the world with these metals, make tools and weapons and walls. Yet here they seem almost pitiful, only an opening move in Job's argument.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Man brings light into darkness—digs deep, searches far. There's something almost admirable in this, the reach of human determination. But Job is building to a turn: all this searching, this bravery in the dark, and yet the deepest thing we need eludes us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The miners work forgotten, in shafts away from the world, swinging in the dark. No one sees them. Their labor is hidden like the stones they hunt. I've noticed how the Lord sees those hidden labors—sees and honors them, even when the world forgets.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bread from the earth—the surface gift, the open secret. Below it burns a fire that transforms stone into riches. There's a picture here of God's hidden order, the fire beneath the ordinary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sapphires and gold dust nestled in stone, unremarked until someone looks. They wait in the rock, patient and beautiful, for eyes willing to search them out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the keen-eyed falcon cannot find the path to these treasures. The sharpest eyes in nature know nothing of it. This is Job drawing a line: human industry goes where even heaven's watchers cannot look.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The proud beast, the fierce lion—creation's mightiest—have not trod this path. Only man, driven by appetite, enters these depths. There is something almost tragic in the picture: our hunger is wilder than any animal's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Man's hand on the flinty rock, overturning mountains—he takes what he will, subjects the earth. His reach is long, his will relentless. Yet all this power is about to seem very small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every precious thing his eye sees—nothing escapes his notice. He could almost believe himself the master of treasures, the one who finds what is hidden. And then the question arrives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He binds the streams, brings hidden things to light—seems almost godlike in his dominion. But Job is setting up the great reversal: for all our mastery over the earth's secrets, there is one treasure we cannot find, one thing that will not bend to our seeking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The turn comes. After all that mining, all that mastery—where is wisdom? The question lands like a stone. Job's whole argument pivots here: the treasure we truly need is not in the earth at all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Man doesn't know its price—he can weigh gold against gold, but wisdom has no market rate. It is not found in the land of the living because it is a different kind of thing altogether. The rules we know don't apply to it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The deep says no, the sea says no—even the vast and ancient powers of creation confess their ignorance. There is something humbling in watching the whole created order admit it does not hold what we most need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No gold buys it, no silver pays its price. Job strips away our usual currencies: wealth cannot touch wisdom. This is mercy, really—it means wisdom is not for the rich alone, but available to all on equal terms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ophir's gold, the onyx, the sapphire—each one precious beyond easy measure, yet all fall short. Job catalogs the world's finest to make a point: the greatest human treasures are as nothing next to wisdom. The accumulation itself becomes the argument.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gold and glass, jewels of fine gold—the comparison almost sounds absurd. But that is exactly the point. To pile up all earthly treasure against wisdom is like setting glass beside sapphires.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Coral, crystal, rubies—each is a word marking something the world treasures. Job lists them like a litany of human longing. And yet wisdom outshines them all, as dawn outshines the moon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ethiopia's topaz, pure gold—even the rarest finds fall short. At this point Job has made his case so thoroughly that the words almost become a kind of prayer, a confession that our measures fail.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The question repeats, deepens. We have to ask it again because our seeking has nowhere to rest. Wisdom is not a thing we can find by the same arts that find silver and sapphires.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hidden from all living eyes—even birds of the sky know nothing of it. We are all equally blind here, all equally dependent on something other than our seeing. It is a strange and humbling democracy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even Destruction and Death have only heard rumors—they too are outside its circle. The powers that seem to know all secrets know nothing of this. It is something beyond even death's reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God understands its way, knows its place. Here is the pivot: what is hidden from creation is open to the Creator. Wisdom belongs to God, was never ours to seek in the way we seek ore and stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He sees to the ends of the earth, under the whole sky. God's vision holds the whole creation at once. This is what it means to possess wisdom—not to hoard a commodity, but to see as God sees, to hold all things in true perspective.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He established the force of the wind, measured the waters—God does not search for wisdom like we search for silver. He has it as he has dominion: by nature of who he is. He orders all things by it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He made a decree for rain, a path for lightning—each one a small wisdom, visible in nature. God ordains not by accident but by decree: the world runs on his understanding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He saw it, declared it, established it, searched it out—an almost tender picture of God's care. He did not merely create blindly; he looked, he understood, he pronounced it good. His wisdom is expressed in every particular.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To man he said: fear the Lord, that is wisdom. After all the searching, all the digging deep, the answer is simple and close—a posture of reverent humility before God, turning from evil. Readers today hear the same echo: when we stop grasping for what is not ours and bow before the One who holds all things, we find ourselves in the presence of true understanding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
